A California night. The Santa Ana—the Devil’s wind—blows in from the east, raging through the canyon like a drunk screaming in a bar. The air tastes of a stubbed-out cigarette. But why complain? The weather is fine, so long as you refrain from breathing. You simply lean back on the sweat-stained furniture—lights extinguished, windows shuttered against the gale—and count your blessings. 

It is another sleepless night: one where every crease in the bedsheet scrapes like a dry razor across a sunburned cheek; where even ten-year-old whiskey tastes of sand; and where quiet women in their kitchens trace the edges of butcher knives, eyeing their husbands’ necks. I wish them luck. 

Tonight, it feels as though if I pulled the coins from my pocket and tossed them into the air, they would linger for a moment, glistening like a net drifting down through dark water. I recall the headlights of the cars parked along the shore, their narrow beams dissolving across the dark surface of the lake; the voices arguing over paperwork; the crackle of the radio; the sheeted body resting on the sand, a damp trawling net beside it. No, she wasn’t beautiful—yet she possessed that fleeting age where youth itself becomes a form of beauty. 

“Taking good care of your clients, Marlowe?”

Relentlessly, the wind drives on. Next door, catching the scent, the dogs begin to howl. Gaunt, furious, and raw-eyed from the storm, packs of coyotes descend from the hills, where nothing remains to hunt.

Inhaled air tastes like a crushed-out cigarette butt, though the climate poses no real issue provided one refrains from breathing. The best option is to sink into dark rooms onto perspiration-stained armchairs, seal the window glass against the gale, and appreciate one's fortune. 

It is another evening without sleep, during which a crease in the bedsheets grates like an unlubricated razor over sunburnt skin, aged ten-year bourbon tastes like coarse sand, and silent wives standing in kitchen quarters trace the sharp edges of blades while staring at their husbands' throats. I hope they succeed. Tonight, the heavy atmosphere suggests that if someone flipped pocket change into the air, the metal would hang suspended momentarily, shimmering like a mesh net sinking through black water. 

Memories return of parked automobiles along the shore, their faint light beams vanishing into the dark surface of the lake, accompanied by arguments over official paperwork, a static-filled radio, a shrouded corpse resting on the beach, and a nearby trawling net that had not yet dried. She was not genuinely attractive, though she had reached that point in life where mere youth serves as a substitute for beauty. 

A voice asks, "Are you seeing to your patrons properly, Marlowe?" 

Without pause, the tempest continues to blow. Detecting a scent, nearby dogs begin to bay. Skinny, angry, their eyes irritated by the storm, packs of coyotes emerge from the hillsides where no prey remains to be hunted.

There was a Santa Ana blowing—that hot, dry wind that comes howling down through the California canyons, suffocating everything in its path. It carried a fine, gritty dust that rasped at the back of the throat and coated the tongue, making every breath feel like inhaling ash from a blast furnace. The air was heavy with heat and static, turning the entire basin into a dry powder keg waiting for a spark.

A wind like that does something terrible to the human mind. It curls your nerves, steals your sleep, and leaves a sharp, metallic tang of misery in the air. All across the neighborhood, residents lay awake in the sweltering dark, tossing against sweat-soaked sheets while dark, volatile tempers simmered behind locked doors. You could feel the prickling tension in the streets—a quiet, violent itching under the skin that made ordinary men want to hit something just to break the oppressive heat.

I sat in my room, staring into the dark, unable to escape the oppressive conditions or the thoughts that came with them. My name is Marlowe, and nights like this have a way of digging up the past. No matter how hard I tried to focus on the present, my mind kept drifting back to a cold, gray beach and the pale, lifeless body of a young woman washed up on the shore. The memory haunted me, her waterlogged silence standing in stark, agonizing contrast to the howling furnace outside my window. 

Up in the barren hills, the relentless storm and bitter hunger had finally broken the patience of the wilderness. Driven down from the scrub brush by desperate need, packs of wild coyotes began slinking into the neighborhood, moving like dust-colored ghosts between the houses. Their high, haunting yips cut through the gale, setting off every domestic dog on the block. Soon, a chorus of frantic, desperate howling echoed through the canyon—a grim reminder that when the weather turns bad enough, the wild always comes down to hunt.

There was a desert wind blowing that night, hot and dry as a furnace breath straight out of the Mojave. It was a severe Santa Ana, the kind that strips the moisture out of your pores and the sanity right out of your skull. It rattled the loose windowpanes of my office, carrying a fine, red grit that settled over my desk and turned the rye in my glass into sludge. In Los Angeles, when the red wind blows, meek little clerks look at their bosses like they’d like to carve them up with an icepick, and every marriage in the county hangs by a frayed thread.

I sat in the dark, smoking a cheap camel, listening to the city twitch. The atmospheric pressure felt like a iron band tightening around my temples. It wasn't just heat; it was an electric, sulfurous tension that made your arm hairs stand up and your instincts scream that a disaster was coming. 

The wind always brings back the ghosts, but tonight it brought back the Miller case. 

Three years ago, during a burn like this, I’d walked into a bungalow down in Echo Park. The air inside had been suffocating, heavy with the stench of copper and cheap gin. Miller was sitting on the blood-soaked linoleum, still holding the heavy brass lamp he’d used on his partner. He hadn't fought the man, hadn't even hated him. He just sat there, staring at the flies crawling across the floorboards, whispering that the howling outside wouldn't stop, that the wind had shoved its way inside his head and commanded him to strike. Looking at him then, I knew it wasn't just a murderer’s excuse. The storm had stripped away the thin varnish of civilization, leaving only the raw, jagged instinct underneath. The atmosphere hadn't just witnessed the crime; it had pulled the trigger.

Unable to take the suffocating stillness of the office, I went down to the street and took the Chrysler up into the foothills near Griffith Park, searching for a breeze that didn't feel like a blowtorch. But out in the canyon, the dread was even louder. The gale shrieked through the dry scrub oak, turning the hills into a giant, crackling tinderbox waiting for a single, careless spark. 

That was where I saw them. 

A pack of coyotes had been driven down from the high, arid peaks, starved of water and whipped into a frenzy by the static-charged air. Usually, those yellow-eyed scavengers are cowards, slipping through the shadows like skinny grey ghosts. But tonight, the wind had unraveled them too. They stood in the middle of the winding asphalt, illuminated by my headlamps, their coats matted with dust, ears pinned back. 

The lead dog didn't run when I rolled up. He stood his ground, lips curled back over pale gums, letting out a wet, guttural snarl that cut straight through the roar of the gale. He stared through the windshield, his eyes burning with a red, feral madness—the exact same hollow, desperate rage I’d seen in Miller’s eyes three years ago. 

I revved the engine, but the beast didn't budge. He stepped closer, snapping viciously at the chrome bumper, driven past the point of self-preservation by the sheer, hostile violence of the night. 

Sitting there in the idling car, surrounded by the moaning brush and the scent of impending fire, a cold wave of existential dread washed over me. The wind proved how fragile we really were. Fifty thousand years of human progress, of tailored suits and polished badges and law books, could be blown away in an hour by a bad draft from the east. Down in the basin, two million people were sleeping with their teeth clenched, waiting for an excuse to claw at each other's throats. Up here, the wild was snapping at my headlights. Under a sky like this, we were all just rabid animals trapped in a dry canyon, waiting for the whole damned city to burn.

I put the Chrysler in reverse, backed slowly down the dark road, and left the coyotes to scream at the wind.

California is often celebrated as a sun-drenched paradise, a land of endless summer, golden coastlines, and silver-screen dreams. Yet, beneath the postcard-perfect image lies a landscape shaped by raw, extreme forces, where nature wears a darker, more dramatic face.

Travel across the state, and you will notice how frequently the landscape borrows its name from legend. Deep in the heart of Death Valley, where the scorching heat shimmers above jagged, windswept salt formations, lies the Devil’s Golf Course—an expanse so jagged and forbidding that locals claimed only the Devil himself could play there. Head north along the dramatic cliffs of the coast, and you’ll find Devil’s Slide, where treacherous drops plunge straight into the churning Pacific Ocean. From the imposing volcanic columns of Devil’s Postpile in the High Sierra to the blistering "Devil winds"—the hot, dry Santa Anas that sweep through the south each autumn—the moniker appears everywhere.

These names are not mere coincidence; they reflect the inherent duality of California. It is a region of violent contrasts, where lush, ancient redwood forests exist in the same state as bone-dry, sun-baked deserts. When the relentless heat settles over the valleys and the horizon flickers like a furnace, it is easy to see why early explorers and settlers felt a supernatural presence in the wild terrain. 

Ultimately, the true allure of California lies in this exact balance. It remains a place of beauty and peril, a glittering paradise forever dancing along the edge of the Devil’s own backyard.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a noir fiction opening in the distinct voice of Raymond Chandler, featuring Philip Marlowe enduring an oppressive Santa Ana windstorm in California.
counterfactuals.output:
There’s a special kind of heat that doesn’t just bake a city; it cures it, like cheap pork left out in a hot smoker. The Santa Ana came howling down through the mountain passes, dry as a mouth full of sawdust and smelling faintly of burnt brush and bad intentions. It hit Los Angeles like a blowtorch aimed at a grease spot, curling the paint on the stucco bungalows and making the palm trees scratch against the neon signs like old bones.

It pushed its way through the warped wooden blinds of my office on Cahuenga, bringing enough desert grit to re-pave Wilshire Boulevard. The little electric fan on top of the filing cabinet was doing its best, but it was just chopping the hot air into smaller, angrier cubes and throwing them back in my face. 

Nights like this, the humidity drops into the cellar and the static electricity gets so thick you can light a cigarette on your doorknob. It’s the kind of wind that makes dogs bite their owners and meek little men in rimless spectacles go home and reach for the heavy iron skillet. Housewives stand in front of open refrigerators, staring at the bread knives and wondering how much trouble a widow really has to go through. 

I sat there in my shirtsleeves, my tie yanked down far enough to expose a patch of damp chest, watching a moth fry itself against the lamp bulb. I had a glass of Old Forester on the desk in front of me. The ice had given up the ghost ten minutes ago, leaving the bourbon warm, flat, and tasting vaguely of copper. My skin felt like a cheap wool suit two sizes too small, and every nerve in my back was humming like a high-tension wire in a gale.

I was just about ready to lock up, head down to a dark booth at Barney’s Beanery, and drown the wind in cold draft beer until I couldn’t hear the sash cords rattling anymore. 

Then the frosted glass of my office door groaned. 

It wasn't a knock. It was just a heavy, sliding weight against the wood, the sound a body makes when the heat finally knocks its knees out from under it. Through the glass, the dark shape looked tall, soft around the edges, and shaped like trouble in a silk dress. 

I didn't reach for my jacket. I reached for the drawer where I keep the Luger, slid it open an inch, and waited for the wind to blow her in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a hardboiled detective monologue about a miserable, sleepless night in Los Angeles.
counterfactuals.output:
Three-twenty-two in the morning. The sun’s been dead for hours, but Los Angeles doesn’t sleep; it just rots softly in the dark. 

I’m flat on my back on a swaybacked mattress, staring at the plaster ceiling. Outside, the neon sign for the residential hotel across the street flickers with a low, dying buzz. *VACANCY. VACANCY.* Every time it blinks, it bleeds a slow, violent red across my room, painting the walls like a fresh crime scene. 

It’s four nights now without real sleep. My eyes feel like somebody rubbed them down with coarse sandpaper, but my brain won't shut off. It just idles high, burning bad fuel. I tried half a bottle of cheap rye around midnight, but it didn't put me under—it just made my ghosts louder and my stomach turn. 

The heat isn't helping. A late-season Santa Ana wind blew in from the desert yesterday, wrapping the city in a suffocating, dry wool blanket. It’s the kind of heat that makes wives reach for ice picks and men snap over a nickel change. The air in this room is stagnant, smelling of hot dust, stale tobacco, and the exhaust fumes wafting up from Wilshire. The metal desk fan on the dresser just pushes the misery around in circles, humming a flat, tired tune that ain't helping anybody.

Out past the grimy window blinds, the city stretches out for fifty miles—a grid of concrete and cheap promises. People come to LA thinking it’s all orange groves and movie starlets, but they don't see the rust under the chrome. They don't see the quiet desperation choking the alleyways behind the soundstages. It’s a city built on celluloid and sand, and tonight, the sand is blowing away.

A siren wails somewhere down near MacArthur Park. It rises, screeches, and fades into the smoggy haze. Somebody else’s disaster taking shape. In this town, a siren isn't an emergency; it's just the background music.

I reach over to the nightstand, my hand fumbling past the cold steel of my snub-nosed .38, and pull a crumpled pack of Lucky Strikes from my coat pocket. I strike a match. The small orange flame illuminates the room for a second—the empty glass, the unpaid bills, the dust motes dancing in the heat. 

I take a drag, hold the smoke in my lungs until it burns, and blow it toward the ceiling. 

Dawn is still two hours away, but it won't bring any relief. Just a bruised, yellow light cutting through the smog, and another twenty-four hours of hunting down other people's dirty secrets for twenty bucks a day plus expenses. 

I lie back down, close my eyes, and wait for the sun. But I know how it goes in this town. The night never really ends; it just gets too bright to see the shadows.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a descriptive passage that captures the atmosphere of Raymond Chandler's "Red Wind"? Include vivid, gritty metaphors about the Santa Ana winds, a memory of a beach crime scene, and coyotes coming down from the hills.
counterfactuals.output:
It was one of those hot, dry Santa Anas that come howling out of the high desert like a breath straight from the devil’s own incinerator. It scraped down through the mountain passes and tore through the city, dry enough to warp a man’s soul and hot enough to bake his bad intentions right through his linen suit. It was a mean wind, the kind that smelled of ash and old copper, peeling the moisture off your skin until your joints creaked like floorboards in an abandoned house. It was the kind of wind that made meek little men want to tear up their marriage licenses and bite cops. 

Out on the pavement, the neon lights didn't glow—they bled into the haze. Even the palm trees along the boulevard weren't swaying; they were twitching, rattling their dead fronds like dried bones in a witch doctor's tin. 

Down in the canyons, the heat was driving the coyotes down out of the scorched brush. You could see them if you looked close enough—thin, yellow-eyed phantoms sneaking past the swimming pools of the big-money boys in Bel Air. They were scrawny as bad excuses, slinking through the manicured hedges with their ribs showing like radiator grilles, hunting for fat lapdogs and reckless cats. Every twenty minutes or so, one of them would set up a howl—a high, wet, crazy scream that sounded like a cheap soprano getting her throat cut in a back alley. 

I sat by the open window, sweating whiskey and watching the dust pile up on my shoes. The heat always brought the past up to the surface, like grease floating on stagnant water. It took me right back to a night down in Malibu three Augusts ago. The red wind had been blowing then, too, hot and relentless off the bluffs. I remembered standing on the wet sand, watching the tide roll in around a dame in a white evening gown. 

She was lying face down where the surf couldn't quite reach her, her blonde hair tangled up in black kelp like gold thread caught in a bird’s nest. The wind had been so dry it had baked the blood on her velvet cape into a dark, brittle scab before the coroner’s wagon could even bounce its way down the coast highway. She had two small, neat bullet holes in her back—precise as buttonholes on a tailored suit—and her eyes were open, staring up at the smog-choked stars with the dull, gray indifference of a spent nickel. The Pacific kept kissing her slippers, but she wasn't going anywhere. 

I poured myself two fingers of rye from the bottle on my desk. The glass was warm. The air was warm. Everything in Los Angeles was hot, dry, and expensive, and somebody, somewhere in the dark, was getting ready to pay for it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Channel 1940s hardboiled crime fiction. Give me a cynical, mood-heavy opening scene rich with sensory details like bad weather, cheap whiskey, hot nights, and the threat of violence.
counterfactuals.output:
The air in the room was thicker than a two-dollar steak, stinking of stale sweat, ozone, and the slow rot of a city cooking in its own juice. It was two in the morning, but the heat hadn't died down with the sun; it just squatted in the corners of my office like a bad debt you couldn't shake. 

Outside, a late-July storm was breaking, but it wasn't the kind of rain that cleaned anything. It was a hot, greasy deluge that struck the asphalt and turned to steam, bringing up the smell of wet garbage and dead dreams from the gutters.

I sat behind a scarred oak desk, watching the ceiling fan slice through the muggy dark with all the enthusiasm of a dying dog. Across the alley, the red neon sign of a third-rate hotel flickered through the Venetian blinds, cutting bleeding stripes across the floorboards. 

I took another drag of a Lucky Strike, the tip glowing like a warning light, and chased the smoke with a slug of Old Crow from a bottle that didn't have a label left to lie about its age. The booze tasted like battery acid and copper, burning a sour track down my gullet, but at three bucks a fifth, it was the cheapest way I knew to buy an hour’s worth of amnesia. 

Down on the street, a siren wailed—a thin, miserable sound that died out before it reached Fifth. Nobody was coming to help anyone tonight. In this town, violence wasn't a surprise; it was just the local climate. You could feel it settling in the back of your throat, heavy and metallic, right before the lightning cracked.

Then I heard the floorboard groan in the outer hallway.

It wasn't the clumsy shuffle of the night janitor or the light step of a dame with a soft story and a hard heart. It was a heavy, deliberate tread. The kind made by rubber-soled oxfords carrying two hundred pounds of bad news.

I didn't turn on the lamp. I just slid my right hand down into the open desk drawer, my sweat-slicked fingers wrapping around the cold, checkered grip of the Colt .38 snubnose. The steel was ice against my palm—the only cool thing in the whole damn city.

The shadow hit the frosted glass of my office door, blocking out the red neon. Then came the soft, metallic *click* of the latch turning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Santa Ana winds blowing through LA, sweat on sheets, cheap whiskey, a murder scene memory, Philip Marlowe internal monologue. Write a short atmospheric piece.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a wind that comes off the Mojave when the desert gets tired of keeping its heat to itself. The Santa Ana. It blows dry and hot enough to warp the wood on a cheap coffin, rattling the Venetian blinds like a handful of rolled dice and making every weak-kneed sucker in Los Angeles think about committing a crime he isn't smart enough to get away with. 

I lay on top of the bed, stripped down to my trousers, watching the ceiling fan slice the thick, dark air into meaningless ribbons. The top sheet was twisted around my legs, damp and clingy as a desperate woman. Sweat ran down my ribs in slow, itching trickles. 

I reached blindly for the floor, my fingers finding the neck of the bottle. Four Roses. The kind of cheap rye that doesn't fix your problems, it just makes them stand in the corner and wait their turn. I took a pull straight from the glass. It scorched its way down, hot and harsh, competing with the heat in the room and winning by a nose. 

The booze didn't help with the heat, and it sure as hell didn't help with the quiet. In the quiet, the wind just whispered the same damn thing over and over.

*3:00 AM. A bungalow off Sunset.*

The whiskey couldn't wash out the memory. It was etched into the back of my eyelids like a bad photograph. 

I could still smell it. It wasn't just the iron tang of blood; it was the heavy, sweet reek of expensive French perfume mixed with cheap cigar smoke and the heat of a dead man’s apartment. He’d been sitting in a plush leather armchair, wearing a silk robe that cost more than my monthly rent, looking like he’d just paused mid-sentence. Except for the two neat, dark holes in the front of his shirt and the crimson pool taking its time soaking into the off-white carpet. 

His eyes had been wide open, fixed on the doorway. They were gray, glassy, and caught the flickering red light of the neon sign across the street. *VACANCY, VACANCY, VACANCY.* A nice, polite way of saying nobody was home anymore.

I took another long pull from the bottle. The glass was warm against my knuckles. 

In this town, when the wind blows hot like this, you can’t tell if you’re sweating out the sins you’ve seen or the ones you’re planning to commit. I poured what was left of the liquor down my throat, rolled over onto my side, and stared at the dark wall. Outside, a gust struck the window frame, hard and mean. Just another night in the City of Angels, where the angels all had dirty wings and nowhere to fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
